newsitem.title: USA: Data show central banks still buying US Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Data show central banks still buying US Treasuries.

text.p: For more than a decade, money supply numbers have come and gone each week with little fanfare.

But in the past few weeks, the Federal Reserve's Thursday afternoon data releases have come under close scrutiny as so-called custody holdings have been on the rise -- seemingly thwarting speculation that foreign central banks have eased up on buying U.S. Treasury securities.

"Around the G7 meeting there was concern that some central banks had either stopped buying or were outright liquidating Treasuries," noted Douglas Schindewolf, money market economist at Smith Barney Inc. But the data doesn't bear it out, he said.
Last week, Fed holdings of central bank purchases dipped by $500 million, but that was preceeded by a $10 billion jump over the prior two weeks following five weeks of declines.
"It may be the start of renewed interest," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp. "You don't know why the (numbers) go up and down; we could only make conjectures."
Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, said the surge in the dollar has played a major part in increasing central bank buying.

"With the greenback rising, it has led to direct purchases from the investment community," he said. "Will it continue? That's anyone's guess. But you can make a case that if the dollar moves lower we could see an unwinding of (central bank) positions later this year.

"But as long as the dollar stays strong, I don't think you will see any deterioration in foreign custody holdings," Flanagan added. "You need either forceful statements from Treasury Secretary (Robert) Rubin or coordinated intervention, or there will not be any meaningful decline in the dollar."
The latest custody holdings data will be released by the Fed on Thursday at 1630 EST/2130 GMT.
Analysts said the market relies heavily on big purchases by central banks, who in 1996 bought some $115 billion worth.
Economists said the Japanese, for one, can't stop buying Treasuries, since they have to do something with the dollars from the U.S. trade deficit with Japan.
Other countries, too, want dollar-denominated assets.

"Central banks figure they want to be with a winning currency and the dollar is a winning currency," said Marc Wanshel, economist at J.P. Morgan & Co Inc. "If you are China, do you want to buy dollars or yen? Dollars, of course."
Other central banks are moving into dollars, too, Wanshel added.
Still, some experts pointed out that a number of central banks could be selling Treasuries.
"Even with the (custody holdings) numbers going up, some banks might be liquidating," said Schindewolf of Smith Barney. "But that's being more than compensated by others."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212 859-1867 ))
"That's hard to replace," Liro said. "If not for central bank buying last year, it's hard to imagine (Treasury market) interest rates being at these (low) levels.
"We are relying on the kindness of strangers," he said.

Earlier in 1997, talk circulated that the Japanese would start liquidating Treasuries, partly to stem the dollar's rise. But the latest custody holdings figures, coupled with a larger amount of foreign add-ons at the recent quarterly refunding auctions, show that central bank buying hasn't slowed. In fact, central bank buying has risen nearly $15 billion since the beginning of the year.
